newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -- Celgene on Synovir, CelSIDs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -- Celgene on Synovir, CelSIDs.

text.p: Development-stage drug company Celgene sees near-term growth coming from yet-to-be-approved leprosy and AIDS-related disease drug Synovir but sees long term growth from a proprietary class of drugs called CelSIDs, its president said.
"The biggest money will come from SelCIDS because the diseases they can potentially address, such as asthma, arthritis, and diabetes are large," Sol Barer told Reuters in an interview this week.
Celgene reported a loss of $0.47 a share for its first quarter, compared to a loss of $0.34 the year before.
Barer noted that as a development-stage company, Celgene will not become profitable until it launches a product.
Its first potential product launch is Synovir, a thalidomide drug for the treatment of erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), a leprosy-related condition.
"Our near-term growth will come from Synovir," Barer said.
Barer says he expects to hear from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration by September on Clegene's new drug application for Synovir for the treatment of ENL.
Celgene filed this NDA in February under orphan drug status. The FDA must respond within six to nine months.
The company expects to file an NDA for Synovir for the treatment of AIDS related cachexia, or severe weight loss in two to three months.
Celgene is also conducting clinical trials for the treatment of oral and esophageal ulcers in HIV-infected patients with its thalidomide drug.
"AIDS patients could potentially take one drug to help several disease states," Borer said of Synovir.

SelCIDs, or Slective Cytokine Inhibitory Drugs, are potent inhibitors of overproduction of TNF-alpha, a protein that helps the body fight disease. Excess TNF-alpha is linked with many chronic inflammatory diseases.
Celgene plans to conduct its first clinical trial of a SelCID this fall. Borer said that the company has not decided which indication will be addressed first.
